You use the subjunctive to express emotions about what others do (me alegra que, me preocupa que, me da miedo que) and to give impersonal advice (es importante que, es necesario que, es normal que).
Long live the bride and groom!
It’s important that you don’t forget the rings.
It’s normal for you to be nervous.
It’s a pity your grandfather can’t come.
To express emotions about other people’s actions: me alegra que / me preocupa que / me molesta que + subjunctive.
To tell “me alegro de + infinitive” (me) apart from “me alegro de que + subjunctive” (someone else).
To use impersonal expressions: es importante / necesario / normal / mejor / una pena que + subjunctive.
To know when NOT to use the subjunctive: es verdad que, es evidente que, está claro que (facts).
To give a short toast at a party.
It’s 17 May, nine in the morning. Mihai is in his suit, in his flat. Kenji, the best man, has come to help him. Mihai is very nervous.
Good morning, groom. Did you get any sleep?
None. I’m worried something will go wrong. What if it rains? What if I forget my speech?
Calm down. It’s normal to be nervous. On my wedding day, I put my shoes on the wrong feet.
Really? Well, I’m glad you told me. I feel a bit better.
Look out of the window: it’s gorgeous sunshine. It’s impossible for it to rain today.
You’re right. Hey, have you got the rings?
Here they are, in my pocket. It’s important that the best man doesn’t lose them, right?
Very important. I’m scared Tama will eat them. Yesterday she was playing with a ring box at the library.
Tama isn’t coming to the ceremony, mate. Only to the reception. Right, and your parents?
My mum has been at Carmen’s for three weeks. I love that they get on so well. But my dad arrived last night.
He’s very serious. He doesn’t speak Spanish and it bothers him that everyone gives him two kisses.
Ha-ha. It’s better if you give him a hug before the ceremony. Parents get emotional too.
It’s a pity my grandfather can’t come. He’s ninety and can’t travel.
Someone needs to film a video for him. I’ll ask Yuki.
Thanks, Kenji. I’m glad to have you as a friend… and as my best man.
And I’m glad you asked me. Come on, it’s ten o’clock. Time for you to get married!
“me lo hayas pedido” = you asked me (perfect subj.)
“es hora de que” = it’s time for
The cry at every Spanish wedding: BEE-ban los NO-byos! (v sounds like b). The whole room answers: ¡Vivan!
dé (give) has an accent so it isn’t confused with de (the preposition). esté and estés are stressed on the final e: es-TÉ.
When you say “¡Me alegra tanto que estés aquí!”, your voice rises on “tanto” and falls gently at the end. Spaniards show their emotions with their voice!
When you feel something (joy, fear, annoyance) about what SOMEONE ELSE does, use EMOTION + que + subjunctive. Even if the action is real, Spanish sees it through the “lens” of your emotion.
Me encanta que se lleven bien.
I love that they get on well.
Me da miedo que lo pierdas.
Le molesta que le den besos.
It bothers him that people kiss him.
Careful, English and Spanish differ! In English we say “I’m glad you ARE here” (indicative). In Spanish: me alegra que ESTÉS (subjunctive). Don’t translate word for word!
The rule from chapter 37 applies here too:
Me alegro de que estés aquí.
Me da miedo perder los anillos.
Me da miedo que pierdas los anillos.
Two equivalent structures: “me alegra que…” (literally “it makes me glad that…”) and “me alegro de que…” (I’m glad that…). Both need the subjunctive.
When you give a general opinion, advice or assessment, use ES + ADJECTIVE + que + subjunctive:
Es necesario que alguien grabe un vídeo.
Es mejor que le des un abrazo.
Es una pena que no pueda venir.
Es hora de que te cases.
Without a specific subject, use the infinitive: Es importante descansar (It’s important to rest, in general).
4. When NOT to use the subjunctive: certain facts
Expressions that state something is TRUE, CERTAIN or OBVIOUS take the indicative, because they talk about facts, not emotions or wishes:
Está claro que va a llover.
Es posible que vaya a llover.
Quick test: ask yourself “am I stating a fact or expressing a reaction?”. Fact → indicative. Reaction, advice, possibility → subjunctive.
5. How to give a toast (un brindis)
At a Spanish wedding or party, someone stands up, taps their glass and says a few words. A simple structure, with lots of subjunctive:
I’m so glad we’re all here.
It’s incredible that you met at a Japanese club.
Let’s toast the bride and groom! Long live the couple!
At the end, everyone shouts “¡Que se besen!” (Kiss!). The couple have to kiss. It’s tradition!
Me alegro de que esté aquí.
Es una pena que no viene.
Es una pena que no venga.
I’m scared I’ll forget my speech.
It’s better for you to rest.
I love that they get on so well.

At the reception, Kenji stands up and gives his best man’s speech. He wrote it with Yuki’s help and practised it fifty times.
Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Kenji and I’m the best man. I’m sorry my Spanish isn’t perfect, but today is a day when we speak from the heart.
I met Mihai three years ago, in my restaurant. He came in alone, tired, and ordered a ramen. I’m glad that evening he didn’t feel like cooking.
Then I met Ana at the club at the library. At first I thought: “What a pity these two don’t notice anything.”
We all saw it. Yuki saw it. Mrs Suzuki saw it. Even Tama saw it. They were the only ones who didn’t.
That’s why I love that today we’re here with both families together: the Spanish one, the Romanian one… and the club family, which is a bit Japanese, a bit Italian and a bit from everywhere.
Mihai, Ana: you don’t need to know everything. It’s important to listen to each other, laugh together and never go to bed angry.
And it’s very important to eat ramen at least once a week. At my restaurant, of course.
Please raise your glasses. Let’s toast Ana and Mihai! Be very happy! Long live the bride and groom!
“os vayáis a dormir” = you go to bed (subj.)
¿Quiénes no se daban cuenta de nada?
Que se escuchen y se rían juntos
¿Qué consejo divertido les da al final?
Comer ramen una vez a la semana en su restaurante
Yuki had a mission: to film the whole wedding for Mihai’s grandfather, who lived in a village in the Romanian mountains and was ninety years old.
She had got up at seven, charged her phone and bought a spare battery. It was important that nothing was missing.
The ceremony at the Town Hall was short but very beautiful. Ana came in on her father’s arm, in Grandma Rosario’s dress.
Nobody knew that inside the dress there was a small hand-sewn blue flower. Only the two mothers crying in the front row knew.
When the judge asked “Do you take Ana as your wife?”, Mihai was so nervous he answered “Hai” in Japanese. Everyone laughed. He went red and repeated: “Yes, I do!”
Kenji took the rings out of his pocket. For one terrible second he couldn’t find them. Then he realised they were in his other pocket. Yuki filmed everything.
Then came the reception in the restaurant garden. There were Japanese lanterns in the trees and flowers on every table.

The food was a success. The Spaniards tried the sarmale and asked for more. The Romanians tried the jamón and asked for more. Everyone tried the cold ciorbă and nobody knew what to say, but they finished it.
Sofía had made a five-tier cake. Right at the top there were two figurines: a bride and a groom… and a white cat between them.
Mihai’s father, Ion, was sitting in a corner, very serious. He wasn’t talking to anyone. Yuki got worried: it was a pity for him to be alone on such a happy day.
Then she saw Ana’s father sitting down next to him with a bottle of wine. The two men didn’t have a single language in common.
Ana’s father poured two glasses. He raised his and said: “Salud”. Ion looked at him, raised his and said: “Noroc”.
Half an hour later the bottle was empty and the two men were laughing like old friends. Nobody ever found out what they talked about.
Later the dancing began. First a waltz. Then a sevillana danced by Carmen and Aunt Pepa. Then the music changed.
Mihai had prepared a surprise: a Romanian hora. The hora began, and Elena took Carmen by the hand. Carmen took Sakura’s hand. Sakura took Kenji’s hand.
By the end there was a huge circle: Spaniards, Romanians, Japanese, an Italian woman and a seventy-five-year-old lady dancing with Tama in her arms.
It was already night when Yuki sat down, tired, on a bench in the garden and checked the video. She had three hours of footage.
Mihai sat down next to her. “Have you got everything?” “Everything. Even the ‘Hai’ at the Town Hall,” said Yuki, smiling.
“Thank you. I’m so sorry my grandfather isn’t here. But I’m glad he’ll be able to see it.”
Yuki handed him the phone. “Call him now. It’s an hour later in Romania, but I think he’s waiting for you.”
Mihai called. On the other end came a very old and very cheerful voice.
“Mihai, my boy! Are you married yet?”
Mihai told him everything in Romanian: the ceremony, the “Hai”, the rings in the other pocket, the hora with Japanese guests. His grandfather laughed so hard he started coughing.
Before hanging up, his grandfather told him something that Mihai later translated for Ana:
“I’m glad you’ve found someone who makes you laugh. That’s the most important thing. The rest can be learned.”
Ana rested her head on Mihai’s shoulder. The music could still be heard in the garden. Tama was asleep under the cake table.
“It’s incredible that it all started with a ramen,” said Ana.
“With a ramen and a great desire to learn,” Mihai answered.
From the restaurant door, Kenji raised his glass towards them. Nobody heard him, but his lips said: “Kanpai”.
